title: Gravitational wave matched filtering by quantum Monte Carlo integration and quantum amplitude amplification
abstract_summary: The paper proposes a quantum algorithm for gravitational-wave matched filtering that replaces the classical FFT-based SNR calculation with quantum Monte Carlo integration (QMCI) and uses quantum amplitude amplification to search templates. This approach dramatically reduces required qubits (polylog scaling in data length) compared to prior quantum methods while retaining a quadratic speedup in the number of templates; it handles QMCI errors by introducing two SNR thresholds to control false alarms and misses.
methodology_description: This is a theoretical / algorithmic study proposing a new quantum algorithm for gravitational-wave matched filtering. The authors replace the FFT-based SNR calculation used in prior quantum proposals with a Quantum Monte Carlo Integration (QMCI) approach and use Quantum Amplitude Amplification (QAA) to search templates with high SNR. The methodology is formal and consists of: (1) Problem formulation and notation for discrete-time SNR computation; (2) assumptions about available oracles and statistical properties of detector data (notably availability of oracles providing real/imaginary parts of preweighted Fourier data and bounded mean/variance conditions); (3) construction of low-level arithmetic oracles (add, sub, mul, div, elementary functions, comparers, controlled rotations, median and uniform superposition generators) and the QRAM-based data loading assumption; (4) derivation of an oracle O_r that computes individual summands of the discrete SNR expression and bounding their variance (Lemma 1) under the stated assumptions; (5) application of a QMCI subroutine (based on amplitude estimation techniques) to estimate the mean of the SNR summands with tunable precision; (6) design of a two-threshold decision strategy (rho_soft, rho_hard) to accommodate QMCI errors, with QMCI accuracy set to (rho_hard - rho_soft)/2; (7) composition of these components into a higher-level oracle O_AE that flags templates whose QMCI-estimated SNR exceeds the midpoint threshold; (8) running QAA on O_AE to amplify and find marked template/time pairs and final classical verification (compute exact SNR via FFT classically for returned candidate); and (9) formal complexity and qubit-count analyses (theorems) that quantify query complexity to primitive oracles and qubit scaling, showing polylog(M) qubit scaling (vs O(M) for FFT-based approach) and quadratic speedup in template count. The methodology is mathematical, proving correctness and bounds (theorems and proofs), detailing algorithmic steps, and analyzing resource costs; no empirical or simulation experiments are reported.

results_summary: This preprint presents a theoretical quantum algorithm for gravitational-wave matched filtering that substitutes FFT-based SNR computation with quantum Monte Carlo integration (QMCI) and employs quantum amplitude amplification to search templates. The key claimed benefit is an exponential reduction in qubit requirements with respect to the number of time bins M (from O(M) to O(poly(log M))) while preserving a quadratic speedup over classical exhaustive template search in the number of templates. To manage QMCI's approximation errors the authors propose a two-threshold (ρ_hard, ρ_soft) strategy. They derive variance bounds for the SNR summands and provide formal query- and qubit-complexity bounds (including logarithmic factors). A numerical waveform/PSD example supports that a problem-dependent constant γ is O(1), reinforcing the stated complexity scaling. The work is theoretical/algorithmic and does not include an experimental demonstration; practical challenges such as the need for QRAM are acknowledged.

quantum_advantage_detail: The paper claims a theoretical quantum advantage: a quadratic speedup over classical matched filtering in the template dimension (Ntemp) is retained, and an exponential qubit-count reduction in M (number of time/frequency bins) is achieved by replacing FFT with QMCI. These claims are complexity-theoretic and algorithmic (no hardware experiments); they rely on assumptions (e.g., availability of QRAM, bounded variance) and invoke known quantum subroutines (QMCI, QAA), so the advantage is demonstrated at the theoretical/complexity level rather than empirically.
limitations: QMCI (quantum Monte Carlo integration) is intrinsically approximate and therefore necessitates a two-threshold scheme (ρhard and ρsoft) to avoid false alarms; templates with SNR in [ρsoft, ρhard) may be ambiguous (author-stated).
The algorithm requires QRAM to load detector Fourier-mode data in superposition; the experimental realization of QRAM is challenging (author-stated).

The method assumes availability of several arithmetic oracles and oracles ORe and OIm (for loading real/imag parts); these are taken as given and constitute a nontrivial implementation requirement (author-stated).

The paper treats only the SNR ranking statistic for simplicity and does not implement more realistic ranking statistics (e.g., χ2 tests) or fully treat non-Gaussian glitches; applicability to production searches with real detector artefacts is not demonstrated (author-stated).
Finite-precision representation errors are neglected (the paper assumes Ndig is arbitrarily large), so numerical round-off / representation errors are not analyzed (author-stated).

The analysis relies on assumptions about the detector noise (Gaussianity, M ≫ 1) and variance bounds (Assumption 2); departures from these assumptions in real data could invalidate parts of the resource/error analysis (author-stated).
Preloading experimental data into QRAM requires O(M) time and memory to initialize the QRAM, which is a practical overhead (author-stated).

[inferred] The paper does not provide concrete end-to-end resource estimates accounting for fault-tolerant overhead (logical-to-physical qubit ratios, error-correction cycles); practical feasibility on realistic future hardware remains unclear.
